problem.text: In the given circle, the diameter $\overline{EB}$ is parallel to $\overline{DC}$, and $\overline{AB}$ is parallel to $\overline{ED}$. The angles $AEB$ and $ABE$ are in the ratio $4:5$. What is the degree measure of angle $BCD$?

steps.title: Where to start: the diameter gives a right angle
steps.body: The statement tells us $EB$ is a diameter, and $A$ is on the circle. An inscribed angle that stands on a diameter is always $90^\circ$ (it is half of the $180^\circ$ arc). So triangle $EAB$ has a right angle at $A$.

your_turn.answer: $90^\circ$, since the three angles of triangle $EAB$ add to $180^\circ$ and $\angle EAB = 90^\circ$.

steps.title: Move an angle across the parallel lines
steps.body: Now use $AB \parallel ED$. The diameter $EB$ crosses both of these lines, and $A$ and $D$ are on opposite sides of it, so $\angle ABE$ and $\angle BED$ are alternate interior angles. Careful: the angle that transfers is the one at $B$, not the one at $E$.

your_turn.answer: $50^\circ$, because it equals the alternate angle $\angle ABE$.

steps.title: Put it together
steps.body: All four points $B$, $C$, $D$, $E$ are on the circle, so $BCDE$ is a cyclic quadrilateral, and its opposite angles add to $180^\circ$. The angle opposite $\angle BCD$ is $\angle BED$, so $\angle BCD = 180^\circ - 50^\circ = 130^\circ$. Check with the last condition $DC \parallel EB$: it makes $EBCD$ an isosceles trapezoid, so $\angle CBE = \angle BED = 50^\circ$, and co-interior angles give $\angle BCD = 180^\circ - 50^\circ$ again. The answer is **(C)**.

wrong_choices.E: This comes from using $\angle AEB = 40^\circ$ as the angle opposite $\angle BCD$ and getting $180^\circ - 40^\circ$. With $AB \parallel ED$, the angle equal to $\angle BED$ is $\angle ABE = 50^\circ$, not $\angle AEB$.
